books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate (March 31, 1876)

stimulus.text:
“I have confidence, not only in this country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunity offers and ability serves, seek our places, sometimes in the field of letters, arts, sciences, and the professions. More frequently mechanical pursuits will attract and elicit our efforts; more still of my people will find employment and livelihood as the cultivators of the soil. The bulk of this people—by surroundings, habits, adaption, and choice—will continue to find their homes in the South, and constitute the masses of its yeomanry.”

—Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate to introduce a resolution appointing a committee to investigate election practices in Mississippi, March 31, 1876
stimulus.source_note: Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate, March 31, 1876. Public domain. Wording verified against the quotation in 5 Steps to a 5, AP U.S. History 2024, Chapter 16, including the book’s spelling “adaption.”

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Bruce, a Black Republican from Mississippi, served in the Senate at a time when

options.text: Black men held office across the South under Reconstruction governments.
no Black man had yet voted in any American election.
options.misconception: Background: Black men had been voting since the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.

options.text: the Democratic Party controlled every Southern state.
options.misconception: Background: Republicans still held several Southern states in the mid-1870s.

options.text: the Fifteenth Amendment had not yet been ratified.
options.misconception: Background: the Fifteenth Amendment was ratified in 1870, five years before Bruce took his seat.

rationales.A: In the early 1870s, hundreds of Black men sat in Southern legislatures, and sixteen served in the House, with two in the Senate. Bruce’s career belonged to that moment, when Reconstruction governments opened office to Black men across the South.
rationales.B: Background: Black men had been voting since the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
rationales.C: Background: Republicans still held several Southern states in the mid-1870s.
rationales.D: Background: the Fifteenth Amendment was ratified in 1870, five years before Bruce took his seat.
rationales.general:
1. Bruce took his Senate seat in 1875, in the middle of Reconstruction.
2. Background: by then, hundreds of Black men held office in Southern legislatures, and sixteen had served in the House.
3. His seat was unusual, but it was not a lone accident.
4. It belonged to a whole generation of Black officeholders.
Remember: one person’s first is often part of a larger wave.
